nh_stonehouse_pond_2.blurb: Stonehouse Pond is a granite cliff of roughly 150 feet above a quiet pond in Barrington, in the southeast corner of the state. The rock is coarse pegmatitic granite, and the walls turn in different directions, so there is usually a sunny or a shady option. Most of the climbing is bolted sport, with a smaller share of trad routes that want extra gear. Difficulty skews toward the 5.11 and 5.12 range, with a handful of moderates and a few harder lines above. Reaching some of the routes means using ledges and steep hillside, so it is not the easiest place to bring dogs, kids or a big group. Bring a bag for your trash and keep human waste well back from the water.

nh_main_wall_the.blurb: The Main Wall is the centerpiece of Greens Cliff, a remote granite crag deep in the White Mountain National Forest. It is a long band of rock, about a third of a mile across and up to around 250 feet high, split by cracks and flake systems with stretches of steep slab, face and big roofs. The routes are mostly traditional, one and two pitches, with most grades falling between 5.9 and 5.12. The wall faces southeast and catches the morning sun, and it looks out toward Mt. Tremont and across to Tripyramid and Chocorua. The walk in is long, an hour or more from the road, so plan a full day and carry a map.
nh_main_wall_the.approach: A long hike in along the Sawyer Pond Trail, then a cairned climbers' path up a ridge to the base, arriving under the right-hand side of the wall.

nh_the_parking_lot_wall.blurb: The Parking Lot Wall is the beginner-friendly sport wall at Rumney, on the schist of Rattlesnake Mountain and right above the big lot. Routes here are mostly easy to moderate, with a good number of grades from 5.6 through 5.10, on face climbing with bigger holds and the occasional crimpy sequence. The easier lines lean back while the harder ones are steeper. The wall gets morning sun and afternoon shade, and the middle dries faster than the edges after rain. It is one of the busiest spots on a nice weekend. A few winter ice lines also form here.
nh_the_parking_lot_wall.parking_note: Take Buffalo Road from the village. The large lot sits directly below the wall, and the trail up begins from there.

nh_main_cliff_2.blurb: Main Cliff is the tallest and steepest face at Rumney, a schist wall on Rattlesnake Mountain that grows more overhanging as you move along it. The climbing is long, sustained sport, and the pump builds with height. Most routes fall in the 5.10 to 5.13 range, with the bulk at 5.11 and 5.12, and a few easier lines at the start. The wall catches the sun early and dries quickly, then falls into afternoon shade. The center stays drier than the seepier sides, and the cliff is also climbable on mild winter days.
nh_main_cliff_2.parking_note: Drive Buffalo Road from the village to the smaller lot a short way past the main one, then take the trail up.

nh_armed_and_dangerous_main_cliff_left.blurb: Armed and Dangerous is the section to the left of the Main Cliff at Rumney, a short stroll along the base from the main wall. The schist here is steep somewhere on nearly every route, and the climbing is varied and pumpy. It is mostly sport, with a few trad lines, and the grades spread widely, with the heaviest concentration from 5.8 to 5.11 and a small number of easier and harder lines at the edges. It makes a good alternative to the more demanding central wall for climbers working through the 5.9 to 5.11 range.
nh_armed_and_dangerous_main_cliff_left.approach: Walk left along the foot of Main Cliff; the path drops steeply, then rises a little to reach the base.

nh_orange_crush.blurb: Orange Crush is a steep schist cliff at Rumney with roofs and technical faces. The left side is nearly horizontal while the right is more vertical, and the left dries sooner than the right. It is almost entirely sport, concentrated in the 5.11 to 5.13 range with a few easier lines mixed in, so it suits climbers who have spent time on steep rock. The wall sits high enough to catch some breeze, which helps on hotter days. Early spring can leave it wet.

nh_1_the_geriatric_walls.blurb: The Geriatric Walls are a collection of short, mostly one-pitch routes on Humphrey's Ledge, close to North Conway. It is a good place to stack up a lot of moderate climbs in a day, with most grades from 5.6 to 5.10 and a mix of traditional lines and some bolted ones. The cliff has a reputation for imperfect rock, though the left and central sections are fairly solid. Crowds are thin compared with nearby Cathedral and Whitehorse. A swamp below makes the place very muggy in hot weather, so it is better on a cool day.
nh_1_the_geriatric_walls.approach: Follow the trail toward the Cake Walk, then bear left at the fork to arrive beneath that cliff.

nh_2_indigenous_wall.blurb: Indigenous Wall is a section of Longstack Precipice, east of Lake Winnipesaukee, where the routes run from about 100 to 170 feet, some of the tallest climbing in the southern part of the state. It is nearly all traditional, with a typical rack going up to a #3 or #4, and grades that cluster between 5.7 and 5.10 with 5.8 the most common. The cliff looks out over Knights Pond and the lake, and it dries unusually fast, so it can be climbed within hours after a rain. Plan on a stiff walk and a steep final pitch of trail.
nh_2_indigenous_wall.approach: From the lot, follow a path between two boulders to a logging track, continue a few minutes to a cairned path on the left, then climb steeply to land near the middle of the wall.

nh_06_campground_boulders.blurb: The Campground Boulders are a group of problems beside the Boulder Loop Trail at Sundown, off the Kancamagus Highway. They sit along the right side of the trail, and the setting is pleasant, with flat landings, a river close to the car and easy approaches, which suits families and mixed groups. The grades run from VB to V8 with a good spread, with V4 the most common, and the area has room for exploring since many boulders are still untouched.
nh_06_campground_boulders.parking_note: Use the Boulder Loop Trail lot just south of the Albany Covered Bridge on the Kancamagus Highway.

nh_1_square_inch_wall.blurb: Square Inch Wall is the first real wall at Echo Crag on the northeast side of Franconia Notch, above Echo Lake. The routes are short, around 50 to 60 feet, and nearly all traditional, and the name comes from how much of the rock can be climbed. Most are moderate, with the bulk between 5.6 and 5.8 and a few harder lines up to 5.12. The cliff is shaded, so it is nice in summer, but seepage can keep it wet well into spring and after rain. Use caution on the scramble along the base, which has wooden ladders.
nh_1_square_inch_wall.approach: A trail leads a short way from the highway, past a boulder tangle, then turns uphill to the base, passing a small bouldering wall on the way.
